title: The Voices We Don't Hear: Teachers Who Gave Up
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: Pondiscio reflects on a Marquette conference where successful teachers pushed back on his claim that teaching has become too hard, and argues that the missing voices are the teachers who quit. Using Ed Boland's memoir, an NPR story about Liz Stepansky, and survey data on resources and attrition, he shows that capable, idealistic people leave because of weak preparation, classroom chaos and ever-growing demands. He cautions that pay alone will not fix this, and that celebrating only teachers who beat the odds is survivorship bias, like pointing to Aaron Judge to prove home runs are easy. His move is to ask reformers to treat attrition as data, as medicine and aviation treat failure, and to make the job doable. The piece belongs in Practice & Culture because it concerns teacher retention, preparation and workload.
points: Hearing only from teachers who succeed distorts reform, because nearly half of teachers quit within five years and their stories are absent from policy conferences.
Boland and Stepansky show that new teachers are often unprepared for classroom control and student misbehaviour, which training programmes barely address.
Higher pay does not fix shoddy preparation, unruly classrooms or the social-service burdens placed on schools.
Pondiscio cites a RAND finding that 99% of elementary teachers create their own materials, and presents curricula like CKLA as relief for that burden.
He reframes attrition as a system failure, not a personal one, and asks what would make more teachers feel successful.
quotes: I suggested to my hosts that what we really needed was one more panel: earnest, well-intended people who wanted to teach but grew overwhelmed and walked away from their classrooms. Their absence from the conversation—not a flaw of Marquette’s thoughtful event but a field-wide oversight—limits our ability to address the issues driving nearly half of teachers to quit within five years.

After one freakishly difficult year, Boland returned to his old job. “I had taken courses in lesson planning, evaluation, psychology, and research. Next to nothing was said about what a first-year teacher most needs to know: how to control a classroom,” he wrote.

By all means, pay teachers more,” I testified. “But don’t harbor any illusions that doing so will solve the problem.” Higher pay doesn’t fix shoddy preparation, unruly classrooms, or the ever-escalating burdens we pile on teachers’ plates as we treat schools as not just academic spaces but something akin to the social service agencies of last resort.

A RAND study I cited in my Senate testimony found 99% of elementary teachers create their own materials, stealing time from honing their craft and working more closely with children and their parents. A 2024 Pew survey showed only 36% of teachers feel adequately resourced; a 2022 NEA poll revealed nearly half plan to quit due to poor school climate.
Other fields learn from failure—medicine from misdiagnoses, aviation from crashes. I urged Marquette’s audience to imagine a panel of teachers who quit—not to shame them, but to learn.
Education reform must weigh frustration alongside triumph. We need convenings where former teachers speak without judgment: their failures and frustration studied, not stigmatized.
